title: Field treatment that safely stops inaccessible internal bleeding

concept.text: The proposed innovation is a treatment that an emergency responder could administer to stop bleeding inside the body when the injured vessel or organ cannot be exposed or directly compressed. It would provide selective, durable hemostasis across a useful range of injuries, including severe arterial and organ bleeding, while preserving the patient's ability to undergo later surgical repair. Treatment without locating or exposing the individual wound is an intended capability. A dressing that requires placement directly onto an exposed wound falls outside this scope.

Conceptual synthesis. Delivery into a body cavity and delivery through the bloodstream represent distinct approaches. A cavity-administered material would need to reach and control bleeding within the treated space. A bloodstream-delivered agent would need to act selectively at injured sites while circulating elsewhere. Evidence for one approach would establish only the capabilities actually demonstrated with that route, injury model, and treatment conditions.

significance.text: Conditional significance. If responders could safely control otherwise inaccessible hemorrhage before surgical access, some patients could survive injuries that currently require urgent operative bleeding control. The direct benefit would be earlier control during the interval between injury and definitive care, particularly where transport or access to surgery is delayed. How much hemorrhage care could move to the point of injury would depend on the range of treatable injuries, the time required for treatment to work, and clinical outcomes.

Conditional downstream possibilities. Durable bleeding control could give clinicians more time to transport, resuscitate, and prepare a patient for repair. Its impact would depend on whether control persists during movement and delayed surgery, and whether treatment preserves tissue and surgical access. Definitive repair could still be necessary. The supplied material does not establish a survival effect, the proportion of trauma patients who might benefit, or a general replacement for operative hemorrhage control.

missing_breakthrough.text: The target capability combines reliable control of inaccessible bleeding with selectivity, durability, tissue safety, and compatibility with subsequent repair. Demonstrating these properties together across a useful range of severe arterial and organ injuries is the central challenge. The supplied record does not establish whether this full capability remained unavailable as of November 1, 2026, because it contains no current evidence survey.

Engineering synthesis. Treatment must act effectively despite limited access to the wound and uncertainty about its location. Concrete barriers include reaching the bleeding region, stopping substantial blood loss, maintaining control until definitive care, and avoiding dangerous clotting elsewhere. Performance across different injury sites and severities cannot be inferred from success in a single model. The intended range of injuries therefore needs explicit definition.

Engineering synthesis. Delivery route changes the safety and performance problem. An intracavity treatment must control bleeding without unacceptable effects on nearby organs or interference with surgical access. A bloodstream-delivered treatment must achieve sufficient activity at an injury while preserving safe circulation elsewhere. Both approaches require evidence that hemorrhage control persists and that treatment leaves later repair feasible. These are proposed engineering requirements derived from the concept.

current_state.text: The reconciled research identifies an April 2024 Surgery article by Dorken-Gallastegi and colleagues, titled Safety of the injectable expanding biopolymer foam for non-compressible truncal bleeding in swine, with DOI 10.1016/j.surg.2023.11.010. According to that research account, the safety study placed an expanding chitosan polymer into the abdomen of pigs with mild closed-cavity splenic bleeding. Seven of eight treated animals reportedly survived to 28 days. One animal was reportedly terminated early and had superficial colonic ulcers. These details are retained as a reported experimental account whose underlying text was unavailable to the supplied review.

Access and verification are limited. The research states that an initial pass inspected the abstract's Methods and Results, followed by a recheck that encountered a journal access response of 403. The source index contains bibliographic information and the abstract URL, with no retained source text or artifacts. Consequently, the supplied review could not independently confirm the polymer composition, injury severity, animal counts, follow-up duration, or colonic findings. This missing-material limitation leaves those details unverified and provides no evidence contradicting the reported result.

Even if the reported details are confirmed, a small safety study involving mild splenic bleeding would establish a narrow experimental scope. The seven-of-eight survival count alone cannot establish a treatment-related survival benefit without the study's comparator and design information. The reported ulcer finding would require its study context to assess severity and attribution. This account does not establish efficacy across diverse lethal injuries, severe arterial hemorrhage, prolonged field use, or delivery through the bloodstream to a bleeding site.

The supplied evidence ends with this dated study account and its access limitations. It contains no documented human or prehospital results, independent replication, or later evidence establishing the full proposed capability. Its limited coverage also leaves the broader state of the field as of November 1, 2026 unresolved.

completion_criteria.text: Proposed demonstration. Blinded, independently replicated large-animal studies should test hemorrhage control and survival across multiple realistic injury sites and severities, including severe arterial and organ bleeding. Studies should incorporate delayed surgery and assess whether bleeding control lasts through the intended delay. Each delivery route should receive its own demonstration, with the treatment procedure and injury conditions documented sufficiently for independent reproduction.
completion_criteria.label: Independently replicated large-animal studies demonstrate durable hemorrhage control across injuries

completion_criteria.text: Proposed measurements. Evaluation should include time to hemorrhage control, continued or recurrent bleeding, survival, thrombosis away from the injury, tissue damage, and feasibility of subsequent surgical repair. A complete protocol would need operational definitions of successful control, acceptable adverse effects, and the required duration of benefit. Acceptance thresholds should be specified before testing. The supplied material proposes this evaluation framework without establishing numerical thresholds or recognized standards.
completion_criteria.label: Report efficacy and safety outcomes against prespecified acceptance thresholds

completion_criteria.text: Proposed clinical demonstration. Multicenter prehospital trials should then test whether treatment improves survival and functional outcomes under realistic conditions, including long transport times. The resulting evidence should define practical boundaries such as supported injury locations, treatment timing, delivery route, and duration before definitive care. Finite studies can establish demonstrated breadth within those conditions. Claims extending beyond the tested range would require additional evidence.
completion_criteria.label: Multicenter prehospital trials demonstrate improved survival and functional outcomes

related_concepts.text: Roster-based synthesis. EMR-01, Reversible emergency metabolic suspension, shares the aim of extending the opportunity for definitive treatment. EMR-03 targets continued blood loss, while EMR-01 concerns temporary metabolic suppression. EMR-02, Neurologically intact recovery after prolonged untreated cardiac arrest, concerns recovery after a prolonged interruption of circulation. Effective hemorrhage control could contribute to some resuscitation pathways, but would not by itself establish metabolic suspension or neurologically intact recovery after prolonged arrest.

Roster-based synthesis. EMR-04, Inexpensive, universally compatible emergency blood replacement, addresses replacement of lost blood's functions. EMR-03 addresses control of the source of loss. The capabilities could complement each other during resuscitation. EMR-05, A portable, broad-spectrum emergency diagnostic system, could help identify internal bleeding and guide treatment. The aspiration to treat without locating the individual wound still leaves a role for diagnosis in determining eligibility and assessing response.

Roster-based synthesis. EMR-06, Rapid reversal of septic shock and its harmful host response, and EMR-07, Broad-spectrum emergency antidote platform, also seek rapid treatment during time-critical emergencies. Their targets are the harmful host response in sepsis and toxic exposures, respectively. Shared delivery or emergency-use constraints would not establish a shared therapeutic mechanism or transferable efficacy.

Roster-based synthesis. EMR-08, Non-surgical rescue oxygenation for otherwise unmanageable airways, addresses oxygen delivery when airway management fails. It could complement hemorrhage treatment in a patient with multiple injuries. EMR-09, Effective early prevention of post-traumatic stress disorder after emergency care, and EMR-10, Rapid, potent non-opioid treatment for severe acute pain, concern psychological and pain outcomes that require their own interventions and evidence.

Roster-based synthesis. EMR-11, Acute rescue and repair of injured vital tissue, overlaps with the need to preserve organs during hemorrhage and subsequent care. EMR-03 focuses on arresting blood loss while preserving later repair. Demonstrating hemostasis would leave tissue rescue, regeneration, and restoration of organ function as separate capabilities to evaluate.

change_log.change: Preserved EMR-03 and its title, and expanded the concept to explain inaccessible bleeding, durability, safety, and later repair.
change_log.reason: The innovation remains coherent despite limitations in evidence for its present availability and supporting experiment.

change_log.change: Separated intracavity delivery from bloodstream delivery throughout the record.
change_log.reason: The approaches impose different targeting and safety requirements, and evidence for one cannot establish the other.

change_log.change: Retained the reported 2024 study's injury model, composition, survival count, follow-up duration, and colonic finding with explicit verification qualifications.
change_log.reason: The research reports prior abstract inspection, while the supplied review had no retained source text and could not confirm the details.

change_log.change: Integrated the abstract-only access history, subsequent 403 response, and absence of retained artifacts.
change_log.reason: These limitations explain the uncertainty without treating missing evidence as a contradiction of the reported result.

change_log.change: Qualified the scale of the proposed clinical impact and the assertion that the capability remains missing.
change_log.reason: The supplied record establishes neither the proportion of hemorrhage care that could move into the field nor availability as of November 1, 2026.

change_log.change: Expanded the proposed demonstration framework with operational definitions, route-specific evidence, safety measurements, and practical boundaries.
change_log.reason: The review identifies these as necessary to turn the proposed criteria into an evaluable protocol. No numerical thresholds were supplied.

change_log.change: Added roster-based relationships and distinctions for every other supplied EMR entry.
change_log.reason: This explains complementary roles while preserving each concept's identity.

unresolved_issues: The underlying 2024 abstract or full article is needed to confirm the reported material, injury model, animal outcomes, follow-up, and colonic findings.
Comparator details, study design, and adverse-event context remain unavailable, limiting interpretation of survival and the attribution of tissue injury.
The supplied record does not establish the field's state or availability of the complete capability as of November 1, 2026.
The intended delivery route, eligible injury range, treatment window, required durability, and acceptable safety thresholds remain unspecified.
The magnitude of potential survival benefit and the proportion of patients who could benefit remain undetermined.

brief.title: Emergency treatment to stop hidden internal bleeding
possible: After a serious injury, an emergency responder could stop bleeding inside the body without exposing or pressing on the wound, even without locating it precisely. The treatment would keep bleeding under control until surgery and leave damaged organs and vessels repairable.
why: People bleeding internally could gain time to reach surgery, especially when transport is slow. Earlier bleeding control could help some patients survive injuries that require urgent surgery today.
Clinicians would have more time to restore circulation and prepare for repair.

sources.showed: This was a safety study of expanding foam injected into the abdomen of pigs with mild spleen bleeding.
sources.cited_for: It supports studying the safety of foam delivered into the abdomen.
sources.not_established: A small study of mild bleeding cannot establish reliable control of severe injuries or a survival benefit.

sources.who: Leon Naar and colleagues at Massachusetts General Hospital and Medcura
sources.showed: Expanding foam injected into the abdomen improved short-term survival in pigs with otherwise lethal bleeding around the liver.
sources.quote:
Intraperitoneal administration of hm-chitosan-based foam for massive, noncompressible
abdominal bleeding improves survival in a lethal, closed-cavity swine model.
sources.cited_for: Foam delivered into the abdomen can improve survival in a severe animal injury model.
sources.not_established: The experiment does not establish lasting safety, effectiveness across different injuries, or benefit in people.

sources.showed: Injected particles that mimic platelets, the blood components that help form clots, reduced blood loss and improved short-term survival after an artery injury in pigs.
sources.quote:
Subsequently we demonstrated that, following femoral artery injury, bolus administration of
SynthoPlate could reduce blood loss, stabilize blood pressure and significantly improve survival.
sources.cited_for: Treatment through the bloodstream can reduce traumatic arterial bleeding in an animal model.
sources.not_established: This pilot study does not establish lasting control of hidden internal injuries or safety across a broad range of injuries.

sources.showed: A different injected particle formulation failed to reduce blood loss in pigs. Some animals developed clots in uninjured organs, and survival fell.
sources.quote: There are no significant differences in blood loss over the time period studied for any of the groups.
sources.cited_for: Treatments intended to promote clotting can cause dangerous clots away from an injury.
sources.not_established: These findings concern this formulation; they do not establish that every treatment delivered through the bloodstream has the same risks.

shown: Massachusetts General Hospital and Medcura researchers improved short-term survival using expanding foam inside pigs' abdomens after severe bleeding around the liver. This demonstrates benefit in a lethal animal injury model.

Hickman and colleagues reduced arterial bleeding with particles injected into the bloodstream in a small pig study. A separate team found harmful clots with a different formulation, showing why bleeding control and safety must be demonstrated together.
missing: Reliable, lasting control across severe artery and organ injuries still needs independent demonstration for each delivery route.
Treatment must keep working during transport and delayed surgery while leaving later repair feasible.
Safety must include nearby organs and circulation elsewhere in the body.
Trials before hospital arrival must establish improved survival and recovery in people.

milestones.label: Independent animal studies demonstrate lasting control across severe injuries
milestones.explanation: Blinded, independently repeated large-animal studies would have to show lasting control and survival across severe artery and organ injuries through delayed surgery, for each route. This would establish breadth and durability.

milestones.label: Benefits and harms meet thresholds set before testing
milestones.explanation: Tests would have to meet preset limits for control speed, rebleeding, survival, clots elsewhere, tissue damage and later repair. This would establish whether bleeding control comes with acceptable risks.

milestones.label: Trials before hospital arrival improve survival and recovery
milestones.explanation: Trials across multiple centres would have to improve survival and functional recovery under realistic conditions, including long transport. This would establish patient benefit and define the conditions in which treatment works.

uncertain: The treatable injuries, treatment window, required duration of control and acceptable safety thresholds remain undefined.
Success inside the abdomen does not establish success through the bloodstream; each route poses different safety and delivery problems.
The size of the survival benefit and the proportion of injured people who could benefit remain unknown.
